title: RAHAB WENT FROM JERICHO’S SHAME TO THE GENEALOGY OF JESUS
paragraphs: RAHAB WENT FROM JERICHO’S SHAME TO THE GENEALOGY OF JESUS

They knew her by what she had done. God knew her by what His grace was about to do. And somewhere between a condemned city, a scarlet cord, and the genealogy of Jesus Christ, Rahab became living proof that your worst chapter does not get to write your final sentence.
There are names people whisper.
Names attached to stories nobody wants told at church.
Names carrying reputations.
Names followed by that uncomfortable silence when somebody discovers what the person used to be.
Rahab had one of those names.

Before Scripture remembers her as a woman of faith, before James points to her as an example of faith expressed through action, before Matthew places her name inside the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ...
the Bible introduces her with words that hurt.
The Hebrew text of Joshua 2:1 says:
בֵּית־אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה וּשְׁמָהּ רָחָב
beit-ishshah zonah, u-shemah Rachav.
Literally, the spies entered the house of “a woman, a prostitute, and her name was Rahab.”
The word זוֹנָה — zonah is not sentimental.
Scripture does not airbrush her history.
It does not pretend the scandal never existed.
It does not rewrite the beginning to make the ending more respectable.
Her name was Rahab.
And she was known as a prostitute.
That is where the story introduces her.
But thank God...
that is not where God leaves her.
Maybe that is why her story still reaches into places polished religious language sometimes cannot reach.
Because some people reading this know what it is like to have a past.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe everybody does.
Maybe you have done things you would give anything to undo.
Maybe people remember the version of you that you are desperately trying to leave behind.
Maybe you still hear old accusations when the room gets quiet.
Maybe you love Jesus now, but occasionally you look backward and wonder...
“Can God really use someone who has been where I have been?”
Rahab's answer is written across thousands of years of redemption.
Yes.
But the answer is even more beautiful than that.
God does not merely tolerate repentant sinners at the edge of His story.
Through His grace, He brings sinners near.
Jericho was waiting for judgment.
Israel had crossed into a new generation. The people of Canaan had heard what the LORD had done. The reputation of Israel's God had traveled ahead of Israel's armies.
And inside the walls of Jericho lived Rahab.
When two Israelite spies entered the city, they came to her house.
The king learned that spies were there and demanded that Rahab surrender them.
Suddenly the woman with the scandalous reputation stood at the intersection of two kingdoms.
Jericho was on one side.
The God of Israel was on the other.
And Rahab had to decide whom she believed.
That is the moment beneath the moment.
This story is not powerful merely because Rahab hid two spies.
It is powerful because something had already happened inside her heart.
Listen to what she confessed in Joshua 2:9–11.
She had heard what the LORD had done.
She knew about the Red Sea.
She knew about the defeat of the kings east of the Jordan.
Jericho had heard the same reports.
But Rahab responded differently.
Others heard and trembled.
Rahab heard...
and believed.
Then came her extraordinary confession:
“The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
Think about who said that.
Not an Israelite priest.
Not Joshua.
Not someone raised around the tabernacle.
Rahab.
A Canaanite woman.
A prostitute.
A woman living inside a city marked for judgment looked beyond the walls surrounding her and recognized the sovereignty of the living God.
She did not have a spotless résumé.
She had faith.
And generations later, when Hebrews 11 assembled that breathtaking gallery of men and women remembered for faith, Scripture did something Jericho probably never would have imagined.
It put Rahab there.
The Greek begins:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη...
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē...
“By faith, Rahab the prostitute...”
There is something almost painfully beautiful about those words.
Πίστει — pistei — “by faith.”
Scripture still acknowledges where she came from.
But now another description stands in front of her name.
By faith.
Her history had not magically become good.
Grace does not call evil good.
Redemption is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The Gospel is infinitely more powerful than denial.
God deals with sin so seriously that the Son of God went to the cross.
Jesus did not die to convince us that sin was harmless.
He died because sin was deadly.
At Calvary, justice and mercy meet.
Christ bears the judgment sinners deserve, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives something no human being can earn:
forgiveness.
Grace.
Reconciliation.
A new identity in Christ.
This is why Rahab's story should never become a shallow slogan saying, “Your past doesn't matter.”
Your past does matter.
Sin matters.
Wounds matter.
Consequences matter.
Truth matters.
But your past is not more powerful than the grace of God.
That changes everything.
Rahab asked the spies to spare her family.
They gave her a sign.
A scarlet cord.
She was to tie it in the window through which she helped them escape.
Then came the waiting.
Imagine it.
A scarlet cord hanging from the window.
Outside, Israel approached.
Inside, Rahab gathered her family.
Then Israel marched.
Once.
Again.
Again.
Day after day.
Jericho's walls still looked invincible.
Perhaps someone inside Rahab's house looked through that window and wondered whether trusting the God of Israel had been madness.
But the cord remained.
Then came the seventh day.
The priests.
The trumpets.
The shout.
The walls collapsed.
Jericho fell.
Judgment came.
But Rahab and those gathered with her were brought out alive.
Do not rush past that.
The woman who once belonged to Jericho survived Jericho's fall because she had placed herself in faith with the God whom Jericho resisted.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers it:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη οὐ συναπώλετο...
“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish...”
By faith.
Not because prostitution saved her.
Not because deception saved her.
Not because she accumulated enough moral achievements to erase her history.
Her faith was in the true God, and that faith did not remain theoretical.
It moved.
It acted.
It risked.
It obeyed.
That is why James reaches back to Rahab when teaching that genuine faith is demonstrated by works.
James 2:25 calls her:
Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη
Rhaab hē pornē.
Rahab the prostitute.
Then James points to what she did—receiving the messengers and sending them out another way.
James is not teaching that Rahab purchased salvation with a courageous deed.
He is showing us the character of living faith.
Real faith does not remain a religious sentence in your mouth while nothing changes in your life.
Living faith bears fruit.
Rahab believed...
and then she acted like what she believed was actually true.
That is where her story becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because it is possible to know Christian vocabulary without surrendering to Christ.
It is possible to share Bible verses while hiding cherished sin.
It is possible to attend church while maintaining a secret life.
It is possible to say “Lord, Lord” and still resist His lordship.
Rahab did not have generations of Christian tradition behind her.
She heard.
She believed.
And when the moment arrived, her allegiance changed.
Maybe that is the question this story has been quietly carrying toward you.
Has yours?
Not, “Are you religious?”
Not, “Do you believe God exists?”
Not, “Do you occasionally read Christian posts?”
Who owns your allegiance?
Because Jesus did not come merely to decorate your old life with religious language.
He came to save sinners.
To call us to repentance.
To reconcile us to God.
To make us new.
There comes a moment when faith must become more than admiration for Jesus.
The King calls us to Himself.
Maybe your Jericho is not a physical city.
Maybe it is the life you have built around something God has been asking you to surrender.
A hidden addiction.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Dishonesty.
Greed.
Secret compromise.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A carefully maintained Christian image covering a starving soul.
Everybody sees the walls.
Only you and God know what is happening inside them.
And perhaps you have been thinking:
“I'll come back when I clean myself up.”
Rahab destroys that excuse.
She did not become an Israelite with an impressive history and then decide to trust God.
She trusted the God who could give her a future she did not deserve.
That is grace.
And then...
Matthew opens his Gospel.
Most people are tempted to hurry through the genealogy.
Abraham begat Isaac.
Isaac begat Jacob.
Name after name.
Generation after generation.
Until suddenly...
there she is.
Matthew 1:5 in Greek reads:
Σαλμὼν δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Βόες ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ...
“Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab...”
Rahab.
Read it again.
Rahab.
The woman introduced in Joshua as אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishshah zonah, a woman who was a prostitute...
is now named in Matthew's genealogy.
She became the mother of Boaz.
Boaz became the father of Obed through Ruth.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And through the unfolding messianic line recorded by Matthew...
comes Jesus Christ.
Do you understand how staggering that is?
Jericho would have known her scandal.
Scripture records her faith.
And Matthew records her name in the family line leading to the Messiah.
She went from a house in the wall of a condemned city...
to the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Only God writes stories like that.
From scandal...
to grace.
Not because Rahab became the hero of the Bible.
Jesus is the Hero.
Rahab needed mercy.
David needed mercy.
Ruth needed redemption.
Abraham needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
Every road of biblical redemption eventually forces our eyes away from human achievement and toward the faithfulness of God.
And ultimately toward Christ.
Jesus entered a human family line filled with complicated people and broken stories.
Then the sinless Son of God walked toward a cross.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Pierced.
Crucified.
And there He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not tell you to save yourself.
It announces that the Savior has come.
That means the deepest question is not whether your past is ugly.
The question is what you will do with Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years believing your scandal disqualified you.
Maybe someone called you filthy.
Maybe someone used your worst season as your permanent name.
Maybe you did it to yourself.
You remember what you were.
God knows too.
And still the Gospel calls sinners to come.
Not to pretend.
Not to perform.
Not to hide.
To repent.
To believe.
To receive mercy through Jesus Christ.
Rahab's story does not give us permission to celebrate sin.
It gives sinners a reason to run toward God.
There is a difference.
Grace is not God approving the chains.
Grace is God breaking them.
Grace does not say, “Stay where you are.”
Grace says, “Come out.”
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes restoration possible.
And perhaps someone reading this has reached that exact moment.
You are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of carrying two identities.
Tired of telling everybody that you are okay.
Tired of hiding something that is quietly consuming you.
Then stop running from the One who already knows.
Jesus is not shocked by the chapter you are afraid to show Him.
Bring it into His light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to write the details publicly.
Or simply:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Let that comment become more than engagement.
Let it mark a moment of honesty.
Somebody scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose hope is Jesus.
And before you leave, think of one person who believes their past has made them unreachable.
You know who they are.
Maybe they walked away from church.
Maybe shame convinced them God does not want them anymore.
Maybe they are smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Or send this privately with four words:
“Please read this tonight.”

Not merely because sharing helps this ministry reach more people—although it genuinely does—but because somewhere in your circle may be a Rahab standing inside their own Jericho, convinced judgment is the only ending available to them.
Let them hear about Jesus.
There may come a night when your old accusations return and you need to remember that Scripture itself contains the name Rahab in Hebrews 11's testimony of faith and in Matthew's genealogy of Christ.
Not as a purchase of God's favor.
Not as proof that you love Jesus.
Not as a replacement for faithful stewardship, generosity, or giving according to biblical conviction.
Grace cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel-centered ministry continue.
do not miss Jesus while reading Rahab.
That would be the greatest tragedy.
Rahab's story is not ultimately about becoming respectable.
It is about the mercy of God toward someone who believed Him.
It is about faith that moved.
It is about judgment escaped through God's mercy.
It is about an outsider brought near.
It is about a ruined reputation that could not prevent divine redemption.
And it points beyond Rahab to the greater rescue found in Jesus Christ.
So when shame tells you, “Look what you did”...
look to the cross.
When the enemy whispers, “Look where you came from”...
remember where grace can take a surrendered life.
When people insist on introducing you by an old chapter...
remember that Jesus Christ is Lord over the pages still unwritten.
Rahab was once known by Jericho for her shame.
Scripture remembers her for faith.
Matthew records her in the genealogy leading to Christ.
And the Savior who came through that unfolding redemptive history still receives sinners today.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
Then live like His grace actually changed something.
Because somewhere tonight...
someone thinks their story is already over.
Rahab's name whispers otherwise.
The walls that witnessed your shame do not get to decide what Jesus can do with your surrendered life.
